synopsis.statement: SHAPE PROBE, NOT A REAL RUN. This is the same atlas.json with every Decision and Mechanism node removed and the density signals rewritten to a decision-poor profile, rendered by the identical renderer. It exists to show how the artifact reads on a subject where extraction finds no decision record: which sections state their own absence, what "The record" says, and what still survives. Every remaining claim is real and pinned; nothing about the subject was invented.

interviewer_questions.question: "How long did this take you?"
interviewer_questions.answer: 47 commits across 7 calendar days, starting 2026-08-04. The defensible claim is not the line count - it is that every boundary in it is written down and I can show you where it is enforced.

nodes.title: Grader ⟂ Runner
nodes.enforced_by: AnswerKeyGrader has no Runner field; SelfCheckGrader is a routed Grader bean with no runner and no verdict at all.
nodes.what_breaks_without_it: "Exercise" silently starts meaning "code", and every concept question, lesson check and SQL query becomes a special case bolted on the side.

nodes.title: Response ⟂ Grading
nodes.enforced_by: Two independent sealed interfaces. Response permits Code, Choice, FreeText, Query; Grading permits TestCases, AnswerKey, SelfCheck, ResultSet. Any pairing is expressible.
nodes.what_breaks_without_it: Predict-output - write code, judged against a fixed answer - would need a special case instead of falling out of Code + AnswerKey.

nodes.title: Engine ⟂ Content
nodes.enforced_by: scripts/check-no-content.sh, run first in CI and in ./test.sh, failing on three independent leak shapes - and it has its own tests.
nodes.what_breaks_without_it: The copyright position the licensing decision was built to avoid, plus a public repo that cannot be shown.

evidence.note: the git check-ignore probe - the rule cannot silently lapse

nodes.title: Machine verdict ⟂ self-rating
nodes.enforced_by: SubmissionOutcome is a superset of Verdict.Outcome with SELF_RATED deliberately outside it, and every competence query filters on outcome = 'PASSED'.
nodes.what_breaks_without_it: A self-rating could graduate an item through the learned criterion, and the readiness numbers would stop meaning anything.

nodes.title: The suite is red at this commit, and the cause is a real bug
nodes.statement: ./test.sh fails at this SHA. ReadinessServiceTest.staleTopicsFlagsATopicNotTouchedRecentlyAndSkipsAnUntouchedOne expected 30 days and got 31. The cause is that ReadinessService takes an injected Clock but then calls LocalDate.now(zone) - the wall clock - for "today", instead of LocalDate.now(clock). Every other site in the codebase (SessionService, ChallengeService, RepDueService, DeterministicOptionShuffler) uses LocalDate.now(clock); readiness is the lone outlier, so the stale-topic day count is wall-clock dependent and the test only passes when run early enough in the day.
nodes.why_it_matters: It is a one-line fix, and it is worth going first on because the whole point of the injected Clock bean is that day boundaries are testable. A reviewer who greps for LocalDate.now( finds it in about ten seconds.
nodes.how_to_say_it: The suite is red at the commit I am showing you, and I know exactly why: readiness reads the wall clock where every other date-sensitive service reads the injected one. It is a one-line fix and I verified it - I would rather show you the commit with the bug in it and the diagnosis than a cherry-picked green one.

interviewer_questions.question: "Does it build?"
interviewer_questions.answer: Not at this commit, and I know why: readiness reads the wall clock where every other date-sensitive service reads the injected one. 466 tests, 1 failure, 5 skipped. It is a one-line fix.

nodes.title: The tracker says the second language adapter is unbuilt; the code says otherwise
nodes.statement: Issue #26 "Second language adapter" is still open. At this SHA the Python adapter, the Python runner, both registries and a submission.language migration are all present and tested. The issue is stale, not the code.
nodes.why_it_matters: A decided-but-unbuilt probe that trusts the tracker alone would report this repository's single most important design claim as still unproven. The existence gate has to be able to overturn the record in both directions: a stated decision is not evidence of implementation, and an open ticket is not evidence of absence.
nodes.how_to_say_it: The ticket for it is still open because I have not closed it, not because it is not built - the adapter, the runner, the registries and the migration all landed in the commit you are looking at.

evidence.output_excerpt: 086c999 feat(language): add Python as a second language adapter (#80)

nodes.title: The front-end domain is decided and specified, and nothing is built
nodes.statement: The abstraction decision names a Component response graded by a headless-browser runner with DOM assertions, and states plainly that the JSON-test-case model does not extend to it. Response permits Code, Choice, FreeText and Query at this SHA - there is no Component, no browser runner and no DOM grader.
nodes.why_it_matters: This is the one place the language-neutral test-case model is admitted not to reach, and the decision says so rather than papering over it. The abstraction's obligation was to not foreclose front end, and it does not - but "not foreclosed" is a much weaker claim than "supported", and the difference is worth stating before someone asks.
nodes.how_to_say_it: Front end is deliberately deferred and the reason is written down: auto-grading it needs a headless browser plus per-exercise DOM assertions, which is a different Grader and a different Runner, and building it would have pushed the first daily session out by a month.

interviewer_questions.question: "What would you do next?"
interviewer_questions.answer: Front end - it is the one domain the JSON test-case model provably does not reach, it is specified, and it is the last named domain still unbuilt.

nodes.title: "Interview soon" mode is decided and not built
nodes.statement: The scheduling decision specifies a re-weighted challenge scoring function for the final fortnight before interviews, dropping the minimum-interval floor in favour of broad recency. Nothing matching it exists in backend/src or frontend/src.
nodes.why_it_matters: It is called out in the decision as "the difference between a tool that trains the captain and one that also prepares him for a specific date" - the one piece of the scheduling decision that is about the actual deadline.
nodes.how_to_say_it: The scheduler has the two halves the decision asked for; the interview-soon re-weighting is the third piece and it is not built. It is a different scoring function, not a different app, which is why it stayed cheap to defer.

evidence.note: the "Interview soon" mode section of the resolution

nodes.title: The build diverges from the written stack decision, and the record now says so
nodes.statement: Decision #2 names Spring Boot 3.4.3 with Spring Data JPA and Lombok. The build is Boot 3.4.7 with spring-boot-starter-jdbc, JdbcClient and no Lombok. A follow-up comment on issue #2 records the divergence on the decision itself.
nodes.why_it_matters: The queries here are read-shaped derivations over two tables, not object graphs, and records already gave the mapping - so the divergence is defensible. It is also a divergence from a written decision, and Spring Data JPA is what entry-level Java postings screen for, so both halves of the answer need to be ready.
nodes.how_to_say_it: I decided JPA and shipped JdbcClient, and I wrote that down on the decision rather than quietly leaving the record wrong. Every query in this codebase is a read-shaped derivation, not an object graph, so the mapping layer had nothing to do.

interviewer_questions.question: "Why not JPA?"
interviewer_questions.answer: Every query here is a read-shaped derivation over two tables, not an object graph, and records already gave the mapping. It is also a divergence from the written decision, which I recorded on the decision rather than leaving the record wrong.

nodes.title: The runner is unsandboxed by design
nodes.statement: A local subprocess with a timeout (sweprep.grader.timeout, default PT10S) and a 1 MB captured-output cap. No container, no resource limits beyond that.
nodes.why_it_matters: This is sound because there is exactly one user running his own code, and the decision that makes it sound is written down along with what changes the moment the app is hosted. Runner being a small interface is the prepared answer to the follow-up.
nodes.how_to_say_it: It is not arbitrary code - it is one user running his own, locally. Safety today is a timeout and an output cap, the decision to skip a sandbox is recorded with what changes if it is ever hosted, and a container runner is a bean swap because Runner is an interface.

interviewer_questions.question: "You execute arbitrary code. How is that safe?"
interviewer_questions.answer: It is not arbitrary - one user, his own code, locally. Safety today is a timeout plus a 1 MB output cap; the decision to skip a sandbox is recorded with what changes if it is ever hosted, and a container runner is a bean swap.

evidence.note: MAX_CAPTURED_BYTES = 1 MB, shared by both local runners
"what actually gets expensive when hosted ... not the database - code execution"

nodes.title: Recompute-on-read everywhere
nodes.statement: Learned state, rep due dates, challenge priority, readiness and the streak (including its repair count) are all derived per request from attempt history rather than stored.
nodes.why_it_matters: Correct at this scale and it removes any possibility of drift between a cached summary and the history it summarises. It is a scaling question if the corpus ever gets large, and "there is exactly one user" is the honest reason it is fine today.
nodes.how_to_say_it: There is no spaced-repetition state to keep consistent, because there is no state - it is derived on read from the attempt history, so there is no second source of truth to drift.

interviewer_questions.question: "How do you keep the spaced-repetition state consistent?"
interviewer_questions.answer: There is no state to keep consistent. Learned state, due dates, priority and the streak are all derived on read from the attempt history, so there is no second source of truth to drift.

nodes.title: The real content is never verified in CI
nodes.statement: RealContentSmokeTest - the test that runs the answer-tell checker over the actual authored corpus - skips itself when no content clone is present, which is always the case in this repository's CI. The 5 skipped tests in the run above are exactly that.
nodes.why_it_matters: It is deliberate: an expected content failure must not wedge the engine's CI. It does mean the content-quality gates, which are the output of five separate tickets, run only where a clone exists.
nodes.how_to_say_it: A green suite is not evidence a named test ran. Those five skips are the content gates, and they are skipped by design - the argument for putting them in the content repo's own CI instead is the one I would make.

interviewer_questions.question: "How do you know your own content is any good?"
interviewer_questions.answer: By measuring exploit rates against a 25% baseline, finding a 41.2% one, fixing it in code and re-measuring. The honest caveat is that those gates skip in this repo's CI - a green suite is not evidence a named test ran.

nodes.title: The engine is built; the corpus it needs is not
nodes.statement: Issues #43 ("Author the AI/ML family, split by shelf life") and #44 ("Author the core and professional tranche, then the selected role families") are both open. The authoring tooling that derives warm-up reps from a reference solution landed at this SHA; the content it is meant to produce has not been authored.
nodes.why_it_matters: The planning map names content authoring as the most likely place this project stalls after the fun engineering is done, and the two open authoring tickets are that risk still standing. Naming your own project's biggest risk is a good answer, not a bad one.
nodes.how_to_say_it: The engine is ahead of the corpus. The tooling to derive reps mechanically is built precisely because authoring five items per problem by hand is the thing that would have killed this.

nodes.title: A machine-specific workaround is pinned in the build
nodes.statement: backend/pom.xml sets an api.version system property for Surefire because Testcontainers' Docker connectivity probe hardcodes an old API version that this dev machine's Docker Engine rejects outright. It is confirmed unnecessary on GitHub's hosted runners and kept anyway.
nodes.why_it_matters: It looks like stray config and is not. Knowing why a workaround exists before someone asks about it is the difference between a defensible build file and an unexplained one.
nodes.how_to_say_it: That property is a Testcontainers probe workaround for this box's Docker Engine, it is harmless where it is not needed, and it is documented in the project notes rather than left to be discovered.

nodes.title: Source cites an issue number that the record does not resolve
nodes.statement: A source comment cites a bare issue number with no explanation of what that issue decided, and the issue itself carries no resolution-shaped comment. The citation is real; the reasoning behind it is not in the record.
nodes.why_it_matters: This is the sharpest degradation case: it is not silence, it is a dangling pointer. The honest output names it as referenced-but-unresolved rather than synthesising a plausible rationale, which is exactly the confidently-wrong failure the whole design exists to avoid.
nodes.how_to_say_it: That line cites an issue number and the issue has no discussion on it, so I can tell you the code references a decision but not what the decision was.
